hints: Think about what degenerate means for the five 3d orbitals when no ligands are present to disturb them.
Recall how approaching ligands along the axes in an octahedral field affects orbitals pointing directly at ligands compared to those pointing between them.
walkthrough:
Picture the isolated ion with no splitting**
With no ligands around, all five 3d orbitals on $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ feel exactly the same environment. That is what degenerate means here, same energy. So on the left side you draw just one horizontal line to represent all five together.

Let the ligands approach and split the set**
Now imagine six ligands coming in along the x, y and z axes to make an octahedron. Orbitals that point straight along the axes are hit head on and pushed up in energy. Orbitals that point between the axes are pushed up much less. You end up with two levels on the right side, a lower level of three orbitals and an upper level of two orbitals.

Place the split levels correctly in energy**
Repulsion from the ligands raises the energy overall, so the centre of gravity of the split set sits above the isolated ion level. Draw the lower set of three a little above or around the isolated level and the upper set of two clearly higher, with a clear gap between them.

Final answer: Isolated $\text{Fe}^{2+}$: one energy level showing five degenerate 3d orbitals.
Octahedral complex: split into a lower set of three and an upper set of two orbitals, with the average energy higher than the degenerate level in the isolated ion.

hints: Focus on the two nitrogen atoms in Fig. 4.1 and what each nitrogen can offer to the iron ion.
Remember how a coordinate bond is formed and how many such bonds one bipy molecule will make.
walkthrough:
Spot the two donor atoms**
Look at bipy in Fig. 4.1. Each of the two pyridine rings has one nitrogen with a lone pair that is not part of the aromatic sextet bonding. Both nitrogens can donate at the same time, so one bipy molecule offers two lone pairs.

Link donation to coordinate bonding**
When each lone pair is donated into a vacant orbital on $\text{Fe}^{2+}$, a dative or coordinate bond forms. Because one ligand forms two such bonds, we call it bidentate, literally two toothed, and it acts as a chelate gripping the metal at two points.
Final answer: A species that donates two lone pairs of electrons to form two dative / coordinate bonds to a central metal atom / ion.

hints: Visualise an octahedron with Fe in the centre and three bipy ligands each spanning two adjacent positions, like three blades of a propeller.
Think about whether the propeller can twist clockwise or anticlockwise and how those two forms relate to each other.
Recall which type of stereoisomerism occurs when two structures are mirror images but cannot be superimposed.
walkthrough:
Build the octahedral framework**
Place $\text{Fe}$ in the centre with six positions around it. Each bipy, shown as $\text{N-N}$, must join two adjacent positions, never opposite positions, because the bite is too short to span trans. With three bipys you fill all six positions.

Draw the two propeller twists**
If you look down the threefold axis the three chelates look like a propeller. In one isomer the blades twist one way, in the other they twist the opposite way. Use solid wedges for bonds coming out and hatched wedges for bonds going back to show 3D shape clearly. The two drawings must be mirror images.

Name the isomerism**
These two forms have the same connectivity but differ in 3D arrangement and are non-superimposable mirror images. That is exactly optical isomerism. They would rotate plane polarised light in opposite directions.

Final answer: Two 3D octahedral diagrams each with Fe centre and three $\text{N-N}$ chelates occupying cis positions, drawn as non-superimposable mirror images (delta and lambda propeller forms).
Type of stereoisomerism: optical isomerism.

hints: Compare the three $E^{\circ}$ values in Table 4.1 and remember that a more positive $E^{\circ}$ means a greater tendency to gain electrons.
walkthrough:
Read $E^{\circ}$ as reducing power in reverse**
A large positive $E^{\circ}$ tells you the Fe(III) species really wants electrons and is easily reduced. Here the values are $+0.77\,\text{V}$, $+0.36\,\text{V}$ and $+0.96\,\text{V}$. The smallest value, $+0.36\,\text{V}$ for $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-} + \text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons [\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-}$, means the Fe(III) cyano complex is least keen to gain an electron. Its equilibrium lies most to the left, so it is the most stable Fe(III) complex toward reduction.

Final answer: $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-}$ is hardest to reduce because it has the lowest / least positive $E^{\circ}$ value ($+0.36\,\text{V}$), so the equilibrium $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-} + \text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons [\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-}$ lies furthest to the left.

hints: Count the sigma bonding regions around each ring C and the pyridine N to decide their hybridisation state.
Think about what type of orbital overlap gives single bonds around the ring framework and C-H bonds.
Think about which unhybridised orbitals remain to form the delocalised system above and below the planar ring.
walkthrough:
Assign hybridisation from geometry**
Pyridine is planar with $120^{\circ}$ angles. Each carbon bonds to two neighbours plus one H, three sigma regions in total. Nitrogen bonds to two carbons and holds one lone pair in the plane, also three sigma regions. Three regions means $\text{sp}^2$ hybridisation for all five carbons and the nitrogen, leaving one p orbital on each atom perpendicular to the ring.

Form the sigma framework**
End-on overlap of $\text{sp}^2$ orbitals on adjacent C and N atoms builds the C-C and C-N sigma bonds of the ring. End-on overlap of C $\text{sp}^2$ with H 1s builds each C-H sigma bond. The N lone pair sits in the third $\text{sp}^2$ orbital in the plane, available for donation to a metal.

Form the pi system**
The leftover p orbital on each C and on N sticks up and down from the plane. Sideways overlap of these parallel p orbitals creates the $\pi$ bonds. Because all six p orbitals overlap continuously, the $\pi$ electrons are delocalised around the ring, just like in benzene.

Final answer: Both C and N are $\text{sp}^2$ hybridised.
$\sigma$ bonds are formed by end-on / head-on overlap of orbitals ($\text{sp}^2$-$\text{sp}^2$ between C-C / C-N and $\text{sp}^2$-s between C-H).
$\pi$ bonds are formed by sideways overlap of unhybridised p orbitals between C-C / C-N, giving a delocalised $\pi$ system.

hints: Identify the electron rich pi system of pyridine as the nucleophile and $\text{Cl}^{+}$ as the electrophile in the first step.
Draw the intermediate formed when Cl attaches to the ring, showing where the positive charge and disrupted aromaticity appear.
Consider how aromaticity is restored by removal of a ring proton and where the second curly arrow must start and end.
walkthrough:
Attack the electrophile**
The delocalised $\pi$ electrons of pyridine act as the nucleophile. Draw a curly arrow starting in the ring $\pi$ system and pointing to $\text{Cl}^{+}$. This forms a new C-Cl sigma bond at the 3-position. $\text{Cl}^{+}$ is neutralised as it gains the electron pair.

Show the positive intermediate**
Attachment of Cl breaks the aromaticity and leaves a positively charged arenium ion. Show the $+$ charge delocalised over the ring, often drawn with resonance forms, with Cl now covalently bonded and the H still attached to that same carbon. Include all lone pairs on N where relevant.

Restore aromaticity by losing a proton**
A base removes the hydrogen from the carbon bearing Cl. Draw a curly arrow from the C-H bonding pair back into the ring to reform the $\pi$ system, and show $\text{H}^{+}$ expelled. The ring becomes aromatic again, giving 3-chloropyridine plus $\text{HCl}$ overall.

Final answer: Curly arrow from pyridine $\pi$ system to $\text{Cl}^{+}$ to form C-Cl bond.
Arenium / Wheland intermediate with Cl attached at 3-position, positive charge delocalised in ring, shown with correct charges.
Curly arrow from C-H bond to reform aromatic $\pi$ system with loss of $\text{H}^{+}$ to give 3-chloropyridine.
